issues.claim: 5. **Tune retention of disconnected circuits.** ... Lower values save memory, but users on unstable networks lose state more often.
issues.problem: The answer omits the .NET 10 circuit state persistence feature (persisting state when a circuit is evicted or paused). It is a relevant mitigation to the retention trade-off and the question claims to hold for .NET 10.
issues.suggestedFix: Add one sentence to ru and en: in .NET 10 component state can be persisted on circuit eviction and restored, which softens the cost of shorter retention. Verify the exact API name in the .NET 10 docs first.

issues.claim: bugLineSets: [[14]] and 'Line 15 is not a defect on its own'
issues.problem: There is more than one defensible answer. The explanation says JSRuntime registers the reference when it is passed to JS, which happens on line 15. Line 15 also re-attaches the map on every render, so it is part of the defect. A candidate who clicks 15 gets marked wrong, and the explanation contradicts itself.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the answer unambiguous. Either accept [[14],[15],[14,15]] and rewrite the answer and explanation to say the defect is the unguarded create-and-attach pair on lines 14-15. Or reword the prompt to 'click the line that creates the reference that is never disposed' and keep [[14]], removing the sentence that line 15 is not a defect.

issues.claim: in a heap dump the number of `RegionMap` instances and JS interop objects only increases
issues.problem: A click re-renders the same RegionMap instance, so the instance count does not grow per click. What grows per click is the number of DotNetObjectReference<RegionMap> objects and tracked entries. RegionMap instances accumulate only per navigation.
issues.suggestedFix: Change both ru and en to say the number of `DotNetObjectReference<RegionMap>` objects grows with every click, and that RegionMap instances stay alive after users navigate away.
